title: The Case of the Book in Two Places
story: The circulation report shows one copy of Hatchet checked out to two students at once. Neither student has ever met the other, and both have the book in hand. Ms. Vega holds both copies on the desk, and the spines are plainly different ages. The older copy was bought in 2011 and the newer one replaced a lost book in 2019. Every item in the catalog is supposed to carry a barcode of its own. The 2019 replacement was entered by copying the record of the book it replaced. Copying a record copies its barcode, and two items then answer to one number. The scanner was tested forty times on known items and misread nothing. Neither student's card has been lent, and both scanned their own at the desk. The system clock agrees with the office clock to the second. A report can only be as good as the records it adds up.
question: How is one book checked out twice?

suspects.why: the 2019 replacement was entered by copying the record of the book it replaced
neither student's card has been lent, and both scanned their own at the desk
the scanner was tested forty times on known items and misread nothing
the system clock agrees with the office clock to the second
a report can only be as good as the records it adds up

answer: Two books share one barcode, so the catalog sees a single copy.
proof: “The 2019 replacement was entered by copying the record of the book it replaced.”
“Copying a record copies its barcode, and two items then answer to one number.”
clears: A borrowed card: “Neither student's card has been lent, and both scanned their own at the desk.”
The scanner: “The scanner was tested forty times on known items and misread nothing.”
The clock: “The system clock agrees with the office clock to the second.”
The report: “A report can only be as good as the records it adds up.”
explain: Nothing in the library did anything strange. Two real books are in two real hands. The catalog has only one record between them, so every true fact about both gets written into one line and comes out looking impossible.

title: The Case of the Log That Read 38 All Week
story: Food in the staff refrigerator spoiled over a week in which the log read 38 degrees daily. The log has a line for each weekday and a space for initials. All five lines read exactly 38, with no variation of even a single degree. All five were written in the same blue pen in one continuous hand. A refrigerator opened and closed all day does not hold one reading for five days. The thermometer inside was tested in ice water on Friday and read 32 correctly. The compressor runs and the door seal grips a sheet of paper firmly. No power interruption was recorded in the building at any point that week. A dial thermometer left in overnight on Friday read 47 by morning. The log was filled in on Friday afternoon from memory for the whole week. A record written after the fact is a memory, not a measurement.
question: Why did the food spoil when the log said 38?

suspects.who: 📝 A log filled in from memory
suspects.why: the log was filled in on Friday afternoon from memory for the whole week
the thermometer inside was tested in ice water on Friday and read 32 correctly
the compressor runs and the door seal grips a sheet of paper firmly
no power interruption was recorded in the building at any point that week
a dial thermometer left in overnight on Friday read 47 by morning

answer: The log was written on Friday from memory and never measured anything.
proof: “All five were written in the same blue pen in one continuous hand.”
“A refrigerator opened and closed all day does not hold one reading for five days.”
clears: The thermometer: “The thermometer inside was tested in ice water on Friday and read 32 correctly.”
The seal: “The compressor runs and the door seal grips a sheet of paper firmly.”
A power cut: “No power interruption was recorded in the building at any point that week.”
explain: The refrigerator really is running warm, and the Friday dial reading of 47 shows it. The log hid that for five days, and it hid it by never being a log. Five identical numbers in one pen is a page somebody filled out, not a week somebody measured.

title: The Case of the Fifty Missing Pencils
story: The order was for two hundred pencils and the supply closet holds one hundred and fifty. The invoice says two hundred and the delivery was signed for by the office. Eight boxes arrived, and every box label reads twenty-five count in bold print. Eight boxes at twenty-five each is the two hundred the invoice charged for. Mr. Hale opened every box and counted what was inside each one. Six boxes held twenty-five pencils and two held exactly eighteen apiece. The supplier changed its packaging in the autumn and kept printing the old label. The closet has been locked since the delivery and only Mr. Hale holds a key. No pencil has been handed out from that closet since the boxes arrived. Six twenty-fives and two eighteens come to one hundred and eighty-six, not two hundred. The count on the shelf was taken from the labels and not from the pencils.
question: Where did the fifty pencils go?

the closet has been locked since the delivery and only Mr. Hale holds a key
the invoice says two hundred and the delivery was signed for by the office
no pencil has been handed out from that closet since the boxes arrived
the count on the shelf was taken from the labels and not from the pencils

answer: Two boxes labelled twenty-five held eighteen pencils each.

“The supplier changed its packaging in the autumn and kept printing the old label.”

Handing them out: “No pencil has been handed out from that closet since the boxes arrived.”
The shelf count: “The count on the shelf was taken from the labels and not from the pencils.”
explain: The delivery was short and nobody noticed, because everyone who counted was reading labels. The school was charged for two hundred and received one hundred and eighty-six. The remaining gap is the shelf count, which also trusted the print on the box.

title: The Case of the Heavier Apples
story: Group C's apples each weighed about forty grams more than every other group's. All four groups drew their apples from the same crate on the same morning. A scale zeroed empty counts whatever sits on it, tray included. The trays from that set weigh thirty-nine grams each on a checked balance. Group C zeroed its scale before the tray went on and not after. Every group recorded the number in the display without adjusting it. The apples themselves were never weighed, only the apples plus something else.

the apples were measured with a caliper and matched across groups to within a millimetre
each group used an identical digital scale from the same classroom set
all four groups drew their apples from the same crate on the same morning
every group recorded the number in the display without adjusting it

title: The Case of the Ride That Grew
story: Priya's bike computer says she rode fourteen miles on a route the map measures at eleven. It has said the same thing on four different rides this month. The map distance was checked twice with a measuring wheel along the whole route. She did not take a detour, and her riding partner's computer read eleven. Her bike has 26-inch wheels, which roll about 2070 millimetres a turn. A wrong setting cannot change the distance ridden, only the distance displayed. The magnet is tight and a loose one would undercount, not overcount. Her partner's computer is set to the wheel size that partner's bike actually has. The ratio between fourteen and eleven is far larger than those two wheel figures explain.

the map distance was checked twice with a measuring wheel along the whole route
she did not take a detour, and her riding partner's computer read eleven
the magnet is tight and a loose one would undercount, not overcount
the ratio between fourteen and eleven is far larger than those two wheel figures explain

A detour: “She did not take a detour, and her riding partner's computer read eleven.”
The magnet: “The magnet is tight and a loose one would undercount, not overcount.”

title: The Case of the Test That Said Zero
story: The nitrate test reads zero every week while the fish hang near the surface and eat poorly. Zero nitrate in a stocked tank that has run since September is not believable. Something is always breaking down waste, and the end of that process is nitrate. The kit's second bottle must be shaken hard for thirty seconds before use. Its contents settle into a layer that will not mix on its own. The class has been adding drops from a bottle nobody has shaken since October. The kit's printed expiry is next June, so it has not run out of date. The tank's filter runs, the heater holds 76, and the water is clear. A sample taken to the pet shop on Saturday tested at 80 parts per million. A reading of zero from an unshaken bottle is not a measurement of anything.
question: Why does the test read zero?

suspects.why: the class has been adding drops from a bottle nobody has shaken since October
the kit's printed expiry is next June, so it has not run out of date
zero nitrate in a stocked tank that has run since September is not believable
the tank's filter runs, the heater holds 76, and the water is clear
a reading of zero from an unshaken bottle is not a measurement of anything

answer: The second bottle has not been shaken, so the test cannot work.
proof: “The kit's second bottle must be shaken hard for thirty seconds before use.”
“A sample taken to the pet shop on Saturday tested at 80 parts per million.”
clears: An expired kit: “The kit's printed expiry is next June, so it has not run out of date.”
A clean tank: “Zero nitrate in a stocked tank that has run since September is not believable.”
The heater: “The tank's filter runs, the heater holds 76, and the water is clear.”
explain: The fish were telling the truth the whole time and the kit was not. The pet shop sample settles it at 80. A result that is too good to be true is worth testing against something outside the instrument that produced it.

title: The Case of the Quiet Reading
story: A phone app recorded Room 4 at 55 decibels, which the report called a quiet classroom. Every teacher who has taught in Room 4 describes it as among the loudest in the building. A sound meter borrowed from the district read 78 decibels at 1:30 that same week. The phone's microphone was clear and the app had been calibrated in August. the phone's microphone was clear and the app had been calibrated in August

the app's own readings during group work on Thursday reached 74 decibels
the report quoted only the six morning figures and left the Thursday ones out

Calibration: “The app's own readings during group work on Thursday reached 74 decibels.”

title: The Case of the Quadrat by the Fence
story: Group B counted 340 fallen leaves in its square where the other groups counted around 90. All five groups used a square frame measured at one metre on every side. All five counted whole leaves only, with torn pieces left out by agreement. All five counted on the same Friday morning within half an hour of each other. Group B set its frame directly against the base of the north fence. Wind pushes fallen leaves until something stops them, and a fence stops them. Leaves pile deep along a barrier and thin out across open ground. The other four frames were set at random points across the open lawn. A sample taken where a thing collects will not describe the ground around it. Group B counted carefully and counted correctly, and its number is still wrong for the lawn.
question: Why is group B's count four times the others?

suspects.why: group B set its frame directly against the base of the north fence
all five groups used a square frame measured at one metre on every side
all five counted whole leaves only, with torn pieces left out by agreement
all five counted on the same Friday morning within half an hour of each other
group B counted carefully and counted correctly, and its number is still wrong for the lawn

answer: Group B sampled the one place on the lawn where leaves pile up.
proof: “Wind pushes fallen leaves until something stops them, and a fence stops them.”
“A sample taken where a thing collects will not describe the ground around it.”
clears: A bigger frame: “All five groups used a square frame measured at one metre on every side.”
Torn pieces: “All five counted whole leaves only, with torn pieces left out by agreement.”
The hour: “All five counted on the same Friday morning within half an hour of each other.”
explain: This is the hardest kind of wrong number to catch, because nobody made a mistake. Group B's 340 is a true count of a real square metre. Where the square was placed is what makes it useless for describing the lawn.
